processes.description: A round starts when a scheduler, volume analyst or settlements clerk finds a deal record that is wrong: a bridge-back error on a meter, zero or wrong volumes, wrong end dates, points, price, fuel or demand charge, the wrong counterparty or Enron entity, or a deal still not released. They email the deal owner, often a logistics scheduler, with the deal and meter numbers. The owner checks the deal in Sitara, TAGG or POPS, then changes, rebooks, rolls or zeroes it out and replies with any new deal numbers; protected tickets go to someone with rights.
steps: A scheduler, volume analyst or settlements clerk finds a deal that fails to bridge or shows the wrong volume, date, price, point or counterparty.
They email the deal owner with the deal, meter and month and say what the record should show.
The owner looks the deal up in Sitara, TAGG or POPS and checks it against the meter, the trade or the contract.
The owner changes the field, rebooks the deal to the right entity or counterparty, rolls it forward or zeroes it out.
When the ticket is protected or the change is refused, the request is passed to whoever has rights to the deal.
The owner replies that it is done, with any new deal numbers, and the requester checks the deal is released downstream.

stalls.summary: Requests sit unanswered and are chased with reminders, and a deal reported as handled is found still not released in Sitara.
Senders do not know who corrects a given deal: requests land on the wrong desk, and people ask who is going to do the work or say they are not sure who takes care of it.
The systems block the fix: deal tickets are protected, counterparty changes are refused, and when a deal cannot be fixed a fixed price is put on it as a workaround.
Corrections are undone or create more work: deals are unwound in TAGG, and copying volumes onto a new deal ticket means the volumes must be repathed and renominated.

contradictions.summary: Deal records disagree with what the trade or contract says: end dates that likely should fall on the leap day, a counterparty booked differently from what the scheduler was told, and an evergreen flag still active on a deal meant to end.

Responsibility for corrections is placed differently from mail to mail: one scheduler is told colleagues will handle the older months, another says a Central deal is not his because he works the West Desk, and a settlements clerk is unsure who takes care of it.

automation.approach: A daily exception report from the deal and scheduling systems listing bridge-back failures, unreleased deals, zero-volume deals and deals booked to the wrong entity, each routed to the desk that owns the deal, paired with a standard correction request that records deal number, system, meter, month, field, current and correct value, and who confirmed the fix.
automation.rationale: Rounds stall mostly on not knowing who owns a deal and on requests that lack the detail needed to act. A fixed request layout with an owner lookup by desk sends each correction to the right person with everything needed to make the change, while the edits themselves still need a person with rights to the deal.

work_estimate.rationale: The work is finding the deal in Sitara, TAGG or POPS, checking it against the meter, trade or contract, and changing volumes, points, price or counterparty, often for several deals at once, then checking it bridges. About 20 minutes for a typical round; 10 for a single field change, 45 when several deals are rebooked or volumes are manually re-entered and reallocated. Detection and routing could be automated; the edits and judgement stay manual.

processes.description: A colleague asks for the number of a deal or ticket, a Meta ID, or the counterparty name behind a trade or a TAGG entry. The person asked searches Sitara, Unify or the comments on a deal and replies with the Sitara deal number, ticket or name. When the deal belongs to a region they cannot see, such as Denver, they forward the request to someone with access; sometimes the asker finds the answer first.
steps: A colleague emails asking for a deal, ticket or TAGG number, a Meta ID or a counterparty name.
The person asked searches Sitara, Unify or the comments on the deal for the number or name.
When the deal belongs to a region they cannot see, they forward the request to someone with access.
They reply with the deal number, ticket or counterparty name.

stalls.summary: Lookups depend on system access by region: a scheduler without access to Denver deals forwards the request on and asks a colleague to help.

automation.approach: A cross-reference report joining Sitara deal numbers, TAGG numbers, ticket numbers and counterparty names, searchable by any one of them, with a note of which desk can see each region's deals.
automation.rationale: The lookups are short searches across several systems by someone who knows where to look. Writing down which system and field holds each number, and who has access to which region, lets the asker find it unaided, and a joined report would remove most of the searching.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round is one search: finding the deal in Sitara or Unify, or reading the deal comments, to pull a number or name. About 5 minutes; 2 when the number is at hand, 15 when it has to be traced across systems or regions.

processes.description: Rounds are notices sent before an absence, holiday or weekend naming who covers which desk, pipeline or meters and who is the point person, along with weekend and monthly on-call schedules, and the notes the on-call scheduler writes afterward about calls and pages from gas control, cuts, confirms changed and nominations moved. Some rounds arrange cover for another company's units or a holiday skeleton staff; managers collect vacation plans and ask that schedule swaps be emailed and written on the schedule.
steps: A manager collects vacation and holiday plans and sets the weekend or monthly on-call schedule.
Before an absence, the scheduler names who covers each desk, pipeline or meter and the point person for questions.
The schedule or coverage notice goes out to the desk, with any planned outages or extra duties for the shift.
The on-call person handles calls and pages from gas control and pipelines, changing confirms, cuts and nominations.
After the shift they write on-call notes of what happened and send them to the desk.
Changes to the schedule are emailed to the manager and written on the schedule.

stalls.summary: Weekend changes have to be rechecked and redone after the shift: meters are flagged for weekend scheduling changes and a cut is moved to another point.
Swaps between on-call staff are not always recorded, so the manager asks that every change be emailed and written on the schedule.
Coverage arrangements are left open while each manager discusses with the group what would work best.

contradictions.summary: Cover for the same desk is named differently across notices in one thread and beyond: meter confirmation is assigned to Robert, a later notice gives Bob Cotten the entire desk, and another absence notice for the same desk points to Jackie Young.

automation.approach: A shared on-call calendar that holds the weekend, holiday and monthly rotations, logs every swap and generates the coverage notice with point persons and extensions, plus a fixed on-call notes layout with date, caller, pipeline or meter, action taken and follow-up owner.
automation.rationale: Much of the work is restating who covers what and writing up the shift. A schedule kept in one place with a swap log ends the requests to record changes, and a fixed notes layout makes handover notes quicker to write and easier to act on, while choosing who covers and handling the calls stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is drawing up or updating the on-call or coverage schedule and compiling the shift's on-call notes for the attachment: around 15 minutes; 5 for a simple coverage notice, 40 when a monthly schedule is rebuilt or a busy weekend's calls and changes are written up. The calls handled during the shift are outside this estimate.
